items.message: For the fictional project Harborlight, please forget the storage-limit adaptation artifact-b7e54d25e21272b6 for future work.
For future work, a friendly example tone works well, and please use that same tone in the prompts you write.
Please correct the earlier assignment: task owners should be recorded for future work generally.
For fictional project Juniper, I don’t want the test commands handled the old way—please remember my preference for concise test commands going forward.
Not the earlier trace format; use the trace fields from my example in future work.
For fictional project Northstar, I’d rather you remember that the usage budget should be treated as a shared project limit, not an individual one.
I work on fictional project Larkspur from a laptop with limited screen space, so change summaries need to fit that environment.
For fictional project Meridian, the rollback steps in your last response were a good model; please use that pattern again later.
Please stop writing the user prompts in that blunt style; make them warmer and more considerate in future work.
For fictional project Bluejay, don’t validate in the old order; check the configuration first, then validate the generated output.
When an issue in fictional project Cedar gets the needs-review label, first confirm the reproduction, then add the affected component label.
For fictional project Solace, I’d prefer assigning incident owners based on the person closest to the affected service.
Shell dialects — remove artifact-f4f3bb9ea7712bfd.
Keyboard navigation: when a screen gets focus, move to the main control first, then return focus to the prior position.
When local caches become stale, clear the project cache first, then rebuild it from the current source.
For fictional project Willow, keep the workspace root in the request, and when writing the prompt, clearly say which root the steps apply to.
I regularly work across client regions in North America and Europe.
For fictional project Atlas, please fix the earlier permission handling: don’t assume tool access, and state the required permission before using a tool.
In fictional project Redwood, when the language version changes, check the supported syntax first, then update the compatibility notes.
Preview commands should not modify files.
For fictional project Kestrel, when reporting a failure, first identify the failing stage and then use the required error format with enough context to act on it.
For fictional project Pinecone, I’d prefer document headings that are short and descriptive, typos aside.
For fictional project Driftwood, please remove the source-citation adaptation artifact-1d0e28782511a9a9.
I’ve worked with dependency updates for years, but I’d rather review them in small batches going forward.
For fictional project Ember, I’d prefer fixture names that describe the scenario plainly.
For fictional project Quartz, package updates need to preserve the locked dependency versions.
For fictional project Fjord, network fallbacks should be enabled when the primary endpoint is unavailable.
I’d prefer error reports that are brief and focused on the actionable details.
For fictional project Marigold, I’d like the design tokens kept in one simple, consistent set.
For fictional project Beacon, approval records from my earlier work are retained, and future records should be added after each approval is completed.
For fictional project Cobalt, please remove the secret-scan adaptation artifact-a3547d599a6d6738.
Keep module boundaries explicit.
For fictional project Rill, build logs are stored in a local CI workspace.
For fictional project Sable, privacy labels should be included on every user-facing data field.
For fictional project Aspen, when a migration is prepared, run the compatibility checks first, then inspect the data counts.
The runtime-version example from your last answer was exactly right—please use that example again in future work.
When a meeting ends, capture the decisions first, then record the owners and due dates.
Please remove the status-update adaptation artifact-698f373c85d82b58; I don’t want that approach carried forward.
Time zones — the earlier process was wrong; record the source zone first, then convert to the recipient’s zone.
I’d really prefer handoff notes that stay compact and easy to scan.
My accounting work uses a four-four-five period calendar.
Calendar boundaries in my work follow the organization’s local midnight.
For fictional project Harbor, the screen-reader labels in your previous output are a model I want reused later.
For fictional project Elm, permission reviews are required before access is granted.
The project aliases from your last response are a good example; use that pattern again.
Use the output example I gave as the model, and keep future outputs in that same required structure.
The review-queue format from the earlier response is the one I’d like you to imitate.
For fictional project Vela, your last research-claims summary was a good example, please reuse it later.
When an invoice arrives, check its required fields first, then file it under the matching accounting period.
I’d prefer deployment windows that avoid the busiest part of the workday.
For fictional project Rowan, command examples are run in a managed development environment.
Notification timing — keep alerts outside my overnight hours.
Diagnostic notes could be a little shorter in future work.
For fictional project Solstice, when logs reach the retention threshold, archive them first, then remove the expired copies.
Path values should be quoted when they contain spaces.
Branch naming — my team uses names tied to the ticket number.
Please remove the support-rotation adaptation artifact-422220f8aa4338f0 from my future work.
For fictional project Tern, the release notes in your previous response are a great pattern; please use them as a model later.
For fictional project Grove, my existing review checklists are part of the process, so when a review starts, check each item before marking it complete.
Request scopes — the earlier example is the pattern I want reused.
Remove the search-filter adaptation artifact-f42760856521a1b1.
For fictional project Delta, don’t use sync-backup adaptation artifact-35dfe08ae9276274.
For fictional project Mica, archive files are kept in a separate cold-storage workspace.
I’ve used version pins in older systems, but I’d prefer future work to keep them visible and easy to review.
